title: Find a Peak Element II
statement:
You get an `m x n` grid `mat` (rows and columns numbered from 0) in which any two cells that share a side hold different values. Call a cell a *peak* when its value is strictly larger than every one of its side neighbours: the cells directly above, below, to the left and to the right of it. Positions outside the grid count as holding `-1`, so a cell on the border only has to beat the neighbours that lie inside the grid.

Return the position `[i, j]` of a peak. When the grid has several peaks, any one of them is accepted. Your algorithm should take O(m log n) or O(n log m) time.
constraints: No two cells that share a side are equal
notes:
## Intuition

Testing every cell against its four neighbours takes O(m·n). We can do better by treating whole rows the way one-dimensional peak finding treats single numbers. The largest value of a row already beats its left and right neighbours. If the cell right below it is larger still, then the next row's maximum is larger than everything in this row, so a peak must exist further down; otherwise one exists in this row or above. Each such comparison throws away half of the remaining rows.

## Approach

1. `maxColumn(row)` scans one row and returns the column of its largest value.
2. Keep a range of rows `low..high` that still holds a peak; start with all rows.
3. While the range has more than one row, take its middle row `mid` and that row's maximum column `col`.
4. If `mat[mid + 1][col]` is bigger than `mat[mid][col]`, move `low` to `mid + 1`; otherwise move `high` to `mid`.
5. With one row left, return `[low, maxColumn(mat[low])]`.

The final cell is a row maximum, so it beats its left and right neighbours. Every time `low` moved, the new row's maximum exceeded the whole row above it; every time `high` stopped on a row, that row's maximum beat the cell below it. So it beats its upper and lower neighbours too.

## Example 1, step by step

`mat = [[1,4],[3,2]]`, so `low = 0` and `high = 1`. `mid = 0`; row 0's largest value is `4` at `col = 1`. The cell below it is `2`, which is smaller, so `high = 0`. Only row 0 is left, and its maximum is in column 1: the answer is `[0, 1]`. (`[1, 0]`, the `3`, would be accepted as well.)

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log m): about log m rounds, each scanning one row of n values.
- Space: O(1): only a few indices.

## Pitfalls

- Compare the cell below the row's **maximum**, not any cell of the row; only the maximum is guaranteed to beat its left and right neighbours.
- Use `high = mid`, not `mid - 1`: the middle row itself may hold the peak.
- Inside the loop `mid < high`, so `mat[mid + 1]` always exists.
- A peak need not be the largest value in the grid.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `low`, `high` | first and last row of the range that still holds a peak |
| `mid` | the middle row being tested |
| `col` | column of the largest value in row `mid` |
| `best`, `j` | inside `maxColumn`: best column so far and the column being scanned |
